s963.content:
Pierina Morosini was the eldest of nine children of a poor family near Bergamo in Italy, who worked in a cotton mill to support them and was a member of Catholic Action. She wanted to be a missionary sister, but stayed home to help her family.

In April 1957, walking home from the mill, she was attacked by a young man who tried to rape her; she resisted, and he struck her with a stone. She died two days later, at twenty-six. She was beatified in 1987.
s963.intercession: Bl. Pierina, pray for all working women. Amen.

s964.content:
Luigi Beltrame Quattrocchi was a lawyer in the Italian government and Maria Corsini a writer and teacher; they married in Rome in 1905 and had four children. Two of their sons became priests and one daughter a nun. When Maria was carrying their last child, the doctors urged her to end the pregnancy to save her life; they refused, and both mother and daughter lived.

They went to Mass together each day, prayed the Rosary as a family, sheltered refugees during the war, and served in Catholic Action and the scouts. In 2001 Pope John Paul II beatified them together, the first married couple to be beatified as a couple.
s964.intercession: Bl. Luigi and Maria, pray for all married couples and families. Amen.

s965.content:
Takashi Nagai was a Japanese radiologist who became a Catholic in Nagasaki after reading Pascal and being welcomed by the Catholic family of Urakami, whose daughter Midori he married. He was already ill with leukemia from his work when the atomic bomb fell on Nagasaki in 1945, killing Midori and destroying the Catholic district.

He cared for the wounded, and then lived his last years in a tiny hut, writing books about peace and the meaning of suffering that moved all Japan, and raising his two children. He was called the saint of Urakami. His cause for canonization is open.
s965.intercession: Takashi Nagai, pray for us, and for peace in the world. Amen.

s966.content:
Chiara Corbella was a young woman of Rome who married Enrico Petrillo in 2008. Their first two children were born with grave conditions and lived only minutes, and the couple welcomed each of them with love. While carrying their third child, Francesco, Chiara was diagnosed with cancer, and she delayed treatment that could have harmed him.

Francesco was born healthy, and Chiara died a year later, in 2012, at twenty-eight, peaceful and smiling. To her son she wrote that we are born and we will never die. Her cause for canonization is open.
s966.intercession: Chiara Corbella, pray for all mothers and their children. Amen.

s967.content:
Satoko Kitahara was the daughter of a university professor in Tokyo, of a family of samurai, who became a Catholic in 1949 after the war left her searching for meaning. She was baptized Elisabeth.

She went to live among the ragpickers of Ari no Machi, “Ants Town,” a slum by the Sumida River, sorting rubbish with them, teaching their children, and sharing their poverty. She died of tuberculosis there at twenty-eight, and was called “Mary of Ants Town.” She was declared Venerable in 2015.
s967.intercession: Ven. Satoko, pray for all who live in poverty. Amen.

s968.content:
Jérôme Lejeune was a French physician and geneticist who discovered in 1958 that Down syndrome is caused by an extra copy of a chromosome. He gave his life to caring for children with Down syndrome and their families.

When his discovery began to be used to find and end the lives of such children before birth, he spoke out to defend them, at the cost of his career. He was a husband and father of five, and a friend of Pope John Paul II, who named him first president of the Pontifical Academy for Life. He was declared Venerable in 2021.
s968.intercession: Ven. Jérôme Lejeune, pray for every child with Down syndrome. Amen.

s969.content:
Élisabeth Leseur was a woman of Paris whose husband Félix, a doctor and journalist, was a convinced atheist who tried to take her faith from her. Instead she deepened it, praying, reading, and offering her long illness and her loneliness for him in silence, without arguing.

When she died of cancer in 1914, Félix found her diary, where she had written that she offered everything for his conversion. Reading it, he became a Catholic, and later a Dominican priest, and published her writings. Her cause for canonization is open.
s969.intercession: Élisabeth Leseur, pray for all who long for the conversion of those they love. Amen.

s970.content:
Marthe Robin was a farmer’s daughter of the Drôme in France who fell ill at sixteen and became paralyzed and bedridden for the rest of her life, unable even to swallow. For fifty years, it was said, she ate nothing but the Eucharist, and each week she relived the Passion of Christ.

From her dark room tens of thousands came to her for counsel. With the priest Georges Finet she founded the Foyers de Charité, houses of prayer and retreat that now exist around the world. She was declared Venerable in 2014.
s970.intercession: Ven. Marthe Robin, pray for all who are bedridden and alone. Amen.

s971.content:
Madeleine Delbrêl was a young Parisian poet who was a convinced atheist until, at twenty, she was dazzled by God. She became a social worker and, in 1933, went with a few friends to live in Ivry-sur-Seine, a working-class town governed by Communists.

For thirty years she lived there as a neighbor and friend to all, serving the poor and writing about how to find God in the streets of an ordinary city. She wrote that ordinary people of the streets can believe that the street, the world where God has placed them, is their place of holiness. She was declared Venerable in 2018.
s971.intercession: Ven. Madeleine, pray for us, that we may find God in the street. Amen.

s972.content:
Antonietta Meo, called Nennolina, was a little girl of Rome who at five lost a leg to bone cancer. She went on playing and going to school, and wrote, or dictated to her mother, more than a hundred little letters to Jesus, to Mary, and to God the Father, full of love and of offering her pain for others.

She died in 1937, at six. In 2007 Pope Benedict XVI declared her Venerable, the youngest person who was not a martyr to receive that title.
s972.intercession: Ven. Antonietta, pray for all sick children. Amen.

s973.content:
Jacques Hamel was a quiet priest of Normandy who served for nearly sixty years, and in his old age still helped in the parish of Saint-Étienne-du-Rouvray, where he was loved by Christians and Muslims alike.

On July 26, 2016, while he was saying Mass, two men pledging allegiance to the Islamic State burst into the church and cut his throat at the altar. He was eighty-five. Pope Francis called him blessed and a martyr, and his cause for canonization is open.
s973.intercession: Jacques Hamel, pray for us, and for peace among all believers. Amen.

s974.content:
Frank Duff was an Irish civil servant who, in 1921 in Dublin, founded the Legion of Mary with a group of women at a meeting of prayer. Its members, ordinary lay Catholics, visit the sick, the lonely, and the poor, and bring the faith to their neighbors, under the guidance of the Virgin Mary.

The Legion spread to almost every country in the world, with millions of members. Duff worked among the homeless and the women of Dublin’s streets, and was invited to the Second Vatican Council as a lay observer. His cause for canonization is open.
s974.intercession: Frank Duff, pray for all lay apostles. Amen.

s975.content:
Catherine Kolyschkine was born in Russia and fled the Revolution with her first husband, arriving in Canada with nothing. She became a Catholic and, after years of poverty, a successful lecturer, then gave everything away to live among the poor of Toronto and then of Harlem, where she worked for racial justice.

In 1947, with her second husband Eddie Doherty, she founded Madonna House in Combermere, Ontario, a community of lay people and priests living the Gospel in poverty and prayer, and she brought to the West the Russian tradition of the poustinia, the place of silence. Her cause for canonization is open.
s975.intercession: Catherine Doherty, pray for us, that we may live the Gospel without compromise. Amen.

s976.content:
Pedro Arrupe was a Basque medical student who became a Jesuit and a missionary in Japan. He was master of novices near Hiroshima when the atomic bomb fell in 1945, and he turned the novitiate into a hospital, using his medical training to care for the wounded.

In 1965 he was elected superior general of the Society of Jesus, and he led it for eighteen years through the renewal after the Second Vatican Council, calling it to a faith that does justice. He founded the Jesuit Refugee Service. His cause for canonization is open.
s976.intercession: Pedro Arrupe, pray for all refugees. Amen.

s977.content:
Cyprien Rugamba was a Rwandan writer, poet, and composer whose songs were sung across the country, and his wife Daphrose a teacher. After a difficult time in their marriage, Cyprien returned to the faith, and together they brought the Emmanuel Community to Rwanda and cared for street children in Kigali.

On April 7, 1994, the first day of the genocide, they were murdered in their home with six of their children, as they prayed before the Blessed Sacrament. Their cause for canonization is open.
s977.intercession: Cyprien and Daphrose, pray for Rwanda and for all married couples. Amen.

s978.content:
Jan Tyranowski was a tailor of Kraków in Poland, a quiet man who lived with his mother and spent hours in prayer, reading the Carmelite mystics. During the Nazi occupation, when the priests of his parish had been arrested, he gathered young men into “living rosary” groups and taught them to pray.

One of them was a young Karol Wojtyła, the future Pope John Paul II, who said Tyranowski showed him that holiness was possible for everyone and introduced him to St. John of the Cross. He died in 1947 and was declared Venerable in 2017.
s978.intercession: Ven. Jan Tyranowski, pray for all who form the young in prayer. Amen.

s979.content:
Eugenio Pacelli was a Roman priest and diplomat of the Holy See who served as nuncio in Germany and as secretary of state before being elected pope in March 1939, months before the Second World War began. During the war, and the German occupation of Rome, many Jews and others were hidden in convents, monasteries, and Vatican properties.

He defined the dogma of the Assumption of Mary in 1950, wrote encyclicals on the Church as the Body of Christ, on the liturgy, and on the study of Scripture, and began the reform of the Holy Week liturgy. He was declared Venerable in 2009.
s979.intercession: Ven. Pius XII, pray for the Church and for peace in the world. Amen.

s980.content:
Giorgio La Pira was a Sicilian professor of Roman law in Florence and a lay Dominican, who lived in a cell of the convent of San Marco and gave away his salary to the poor. He helped write the Italian Constitution after the Second World War.

As mayor of Florence he gave homes to the poor and work to the unemployed, and he invited mayors and leaders from both sides of the Cold War, and from the Muslim, Jewish, and Christian worlds, to Florence to talk of peace. He was declared Venerable in 2018.
s980.intercession: Ven. Giorgio La Pira, pray for all who serve in public life. Amen.

s981.content:
Robert Schuman was a lawyer of Lorraine, on the border of France and Germany, who served twice as prime minister of France and as foreign minister. A man of daily Mass and prayer, he never married, and lived simply.

After two world wars between France and Germany, he proposed in 1950 to place their coal and steel under a common authority, so that war between them would become “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.” The Schuman Declaration began the European Union, and he is called the father of Europe. He was declared Venerable in 2021.
s981.intercession: Ven. Robert Schuman, pray for peace among the nations. Amen.

s982.content:
Montserrat Grases was a cheerful girl of Barcelona, the second of nine children, who loved music, dancing, and the mountains, and joined Opus Dei at sixteen.

At seventeen she was diagnosed with bone cancer. She bore months of pain with joy and serenity, praying and smiling, concerned more for her family and friends than for herself, and she died in 1959, at seventeen. She was declared Venerable in 2016.
s982.intercession: Ven. Montserrat, pray for all young people who are sick. Amen.

s983.content:
Francis Xavier Nguyễn Văn Thuận was named coadjutor archbishop of Saigon in 1975, days before the city fell to the Communists. He was arrested and spent thirteen years in prison, nine of them in solitary confinement.

In prison he said Mass with three drops of wine in the palm of his hand, made a cross from scraps of wood, and wrote messages of hope on scraps of paper smuggled out by a child, later published as The Road of Hope. Released in 1988 and exiled, he served in Rome, was made a cardinal, and preached of “living the present moment” with love. He was declared Venerable in 2017.
s983.intercession: Ven. Francis Xavier, pray for all who are imprisoned for their faith. Amen.

s984.content:
Mutien-Marie was a blacksmith’s son of Belgium who became a Brother of the Christian Schools. As a young teacher he was so poor at keeping order and teaching that his superiors thought of sending him away.

Instead he was given humble tasks at the school in Malonne, supervising, teaching drawing and music, and he did them faithfully for almost sixty years, praying constantly, the Rosary always in his hand. The boys called him “the brother who is always praying.” He was canonized in 1989.
s984.intercession: St. Mutien-Marie, pray for all teachers. Amen.

s985.content:
Michael Rua was a boy of Turin who met St. John Bosco when he was eight, and Don Bosco told him, “We will go halves.” He became Don Bosco’s first Salesian and his right hand, and was ordained a priest in 1860.

After Don Bosco’s death in 1888 he led the Salesians for twenty-two years, and they grew from a few hundred to thousands, spreading across the world. He was beatified in 1972.
s985.intercession: Bl. Michael Rua, pray for all who work with young people. Amen.

s986.content:
John Baptist Scalabrini was bishop of Piacenza in Italy, a great teacher of the catechism, whom Pope Pius IX called the apostle of the catechism. At the railway station of Milan he saw hundreds of emigrants waiting to leave for the Americas, and was moved by their poverty and abandonment.

In 1887 he founded the Missionaries of St. Charles, the Scalabrinians, and later the Missionary Sisters, to care for migrants on their journeys and in their new countries. He traveled to the United States and Brazil to visit them. He was canonized in 2022.
s986.intercession: St. John Baptist Scalabrini, pray for all migrants and refugees. Amen.

s987.content:
María Romero was born in Nicaragua and became a Salesian Sister. She was sent to Costa Rica, where she spent most of her life teaching music and art to rich girls in a school, and teaching them in turn to serve the poor.

She founded clinics, a school, and a whole village of homes for poor families in San José, and was called the social apostle of Costa Rica. She was beatified in 2002, the first person of Central America to be beatified.
s987.intercession: Bl. María, pray for us, that we may serve the poor with joy. Amen.

s988.content:
Arcangelo Tadini was a parish priest of Botticino near Brescia in Italy, lame from an accident in his youth. He saw the young women of his parish going to work in the new factories, far from home and without protection.

He built a spinning mill and a home for them, and in 1900 founded the Worker Sisters of the Holy House of Nazareth, sisters who worked beside the women in the factories, in the spirit of Jesus the carpenter. He was canonized in 2009.
s988.intercession: St. Arcangelo, pray for all who work in factories. Amen.

s989.content:
Marie-Alphonsine Ghattas was born in Jerusalem and joined the Sisters of St. Joseph of the Apparition. She received visions of the Virgin Mary, who asked her to found a congregation of Arab sisters.

In 1880 she founded the Dominican Sisters of the Most Holy Rosary of Jerusalem, the Rosary Sisters, the first congregation founded in the Holy Land, who teach and serve the people of the Middle East. She was canonized in 2015, among the first saints of modern Palestine.
s989.intercession: St. Marie-Alphonsine, pray for peace in the Holy Land. Amen.

s990.content:
Philip Rinaldi was a farm boy of Piedmont whom St. John Bosco persuaded to become a priest; Don Bosco once told him, “You will be a priest.” He became a Salesian, led the Salesians in Spain, and in 1922 became the third successor of Don Bosco.

He founded the Volunteers of Don Bosco, a secular institute for women living consecrated lives in the world, and encouraged the Salesians’ missions across the world. He was beatified in 1990.
s990.intercession: Bl. Philip, pray for us, that we may answer God’s call. Amen.

s991.content:
Artémides Zatti was born in Italy and emigrated with his family to Argentina at sixteen. He wanted to be a Salesian priest, but fell ill with tuberculosis; he promised Our Lady that if he was healed, he would give his life to the sick. He was healed.

He became a Salesian brother, and for forty years ran the hospital and pharmacy of Viedma in Patagonia, riding his bicycle through the town to visit the sick and the poor, day and night. He was canonized in 2022.
s991.intercession: St. Artémides, pray for all nurses and all the sick. Amen.

s992.content:
Guadalupe Ortiz de Landázuri was a chemist of Madrid, one of the first women to study chemistry in Spain, who met St. Josemaría Escrivá in 1944 and joined Opus Dei. She helped begin its work in Mexico, and later in Rome, then returned to Spain to teach and do research.

She suffered for years from a heart condition, and died in 1975, smiling. She was beatified in 2019, the first lay member of Opus Dei to be beatified.
s992.intercession: Bl. Guadalupe, pray for all who seek God in their work. Amen.
